Reflect on three things and you will not come to sin: know what is above you—an Eye that sees, an Ear that hears, and all your deeds are written in a book.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabban Gamliel, son of Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, says: Torah study is good together with an occupation, for the effort of both makes sin forgotten. Any Torah study not accompanied by work will ultimately cease and lead to sin. All who labor for the community should do so for the sake of Heaven, for the merit of the ancestors supports them and their righteousness endures forever. As for you, I credit you with a great reward as though you had accomplished it yourselves.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Be cautious with the governing authorities, for they draw a person close only for their own needs. They appear as friends when it benefits them, but they do not stand by a person in time of distress.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Make His will your will, so that He may make your will His will. Set aside your will before His will, so that He may set aside the will of others before yours. Hillel says: Do not separate yourself from the community. Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death. Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place. Do not say of something that it cannot be heard, for in the end it will be heard. And do not say, “When I have free time I will study,” for perhaps you will never have free time.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: An uncultivated person cannot fear sin; an ignorant person cannot be truly pious; a shy person does not learn; an impatient person cannot teach; and not everyone who engages greatly in business becomes wise. In a place where there are no worthy people, strive to be a worthy person.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He also saw a skull floating on the water. He said to it: Because you drowned others, they drowned you; and in the end those who drowned you will themselves be drowned.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: The more flesh, the more worms; the more possessions, the more worry; the more wives, the more sorcery; the more maidservants, the more immorality; the more servants, the more theft. The more Torah, the more life; the more study, the more wisdom; the more counsel, the more understanding; the more charity, the more peace. One who acquires a good name acquires it for himself; one who acquires words of Torah acquires life in the World to Come.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai received the tradition from Hillel and Shammai. He would say: If you have learned much Torah, do not take credit for yourself, for this is what you were created to do.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai had five disciples: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arach. He would recount their praises: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus is a plastered cistern that loses not a drop; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah—happy is she who bore him; Rabbi Yose the Priest is pious; Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel fears sin; and Rabbi Elazar ben Arach is an ever-flowing spring. He would say: If all the sages of Israel were on one side of a scale and Eliezer ben Hyrcanus on the other, he would outweigh them all. Abba Shaul said in his name: if all the sages of Israel, including Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, were on one side and Elazar ben Arach on the other, he would outweigh them all. He said to them: Go and see what is the good path to which a person should cling. Rabbi Eliezer says: a good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua: a good friend. Rabbi Yose: a good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon: one who foresees consequences. Rabbi Elazar: a good heart. He said: I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arach, for your words are included in his. He then said: Go and see what is the evil path from which a person should distance himself. Rabbi Eliezer: an evil eye. Rabbi Yehoshua: a bad friend. Rabbi Yose: a bad neighbor. Rabbi Shimon: one who borrows and does not repay—for borrowing from a person is like borrowing from the Omnipresent, as it says, “The wicked borrows and does not repay, but the righteous is gracious and gives.” Rabbi Elazar: an evil heart. He said: I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arach, for your words are included in his.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: They each said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: Let the honor of your fellow be as dear to you as your own; do not be easily angered; and repent one day before your death. Warm yourself by the fire of the sages, but beware of their glowing coals lest you be burned, for their bite is the bite of a fox, their sting the sting of a scorpion, their hiss the hiss of a fiery serpent, and all their words are like burning coals.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yehoshua says: An evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred of people drive a person from the world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yose says: Let your fellow’s property be as dear to you as your own. Prepare yourself to study Torah, for it does not come to you as an inheritance. Let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon says: Be careful in reciting the Shema and in prayer. When you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine, but rather a plea for mercy and supplication before the Omnipresent, as it says: “For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abundant in kindness, and relents from evil.” And do not regard yourself as wicked.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar says: Be diligent in learning Torah; know what to answer an unbeliever; know before Whom you labor; and know that your Employer is faithful to pay you the reward for your work.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Tarfon says: The day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy, the reward is great, and the Master of the house presses.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to withdraw from it. If you have learned much Torah, you will be given much reward, and your Employer is faithful to pay you the reward for your labor. Know that the reward of the righteous is reserved for the future.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanania ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: “The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: All Israel has a share in the World to Come, as it is said: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever—the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take pride.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Chapter Three
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Akavya ben Mahalalel says: Reflect on three things and you will not come to sin. Know from where you came, where you are going, and before Whom you are destined to give judgment and account. From where did you come? From a putrid drop. Where are you going? To a place of dust, worms, and maggots. Before Whom will you give judgment and account? Before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanina, deputy High Priest, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for fear of it, people would swallow one another alive.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon says: If two sit together and no words of Torah pass between them, this is a gathering of scoffers, as it says: “Nor sat in the seat of scoffers.” But if two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Divine Presence rests among them, as it says: “Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another, and the Lord listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before Him for those who fear the Lord and think upon His name.” This teaches about two; from where do we know even one who sits and studies Torah has a reward fixed by the Holy One, blessed be He? As it says: “Let him sit alone and be silent, for he has taken it upon himself.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon says: Three who ate at one table and did not speak words of Torah over it are as though they ate from sacrifices to the dead, as it says: “For all tables are full of vomit and filth, without the Omnipresent.” But three who ate at one table and spoke words of Torah over it are as though they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, as it says: “He said to me: This is the table that is before the Lord.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanina ben Hakhinai says: One who stays awake at night, walks alone on the road, and turns his heart to idleness is regarded as endangering his own life.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKanah says: Whoever accepts upon himself the yoke of Torah is relieved of the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly burdens; whoever casts off the yoke of Torah is given the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly burdens.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Halafta of Kfar Hananiah says: When ten sit and engage in Torah, the Divine Presence rests among them, as it says: “God stands in the congregation of God.” From where even five? “He founded His band upon the earth.” From where even three? “In the midst of judges He judges.” From where even two? “Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another, and the Lord listened and heard.” From where even one? “In every place where I cause My name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar of Bartota says: Give Him from what is His, for you and yours are His. So David says: “For everything is from You, and from Your hand we have given to You.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon says: One who walks on the road while reviewing his studies, interrupts his learning, and says, “How beautiful is this tree! How beautiful is this plowed field!” is regarded by Scripture as though he endangered his own life.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Yannai says in the name of Rabbi Meir: Whoever forgets one thing from his learning is regarded by Scripture as though he endangered his life, as it says: “Only take care and guard your soul greatly, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen.” Might this include one whose learning became too difficult for him? Scripture says: “And lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life.” Thus he is not liable unless he deliberately removes them from his heart.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa says: Whoever’s fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures; whoever’s wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Whoever’s deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom endures; whoever’s wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom does not endure.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Whoever is pleasing to people is pleasing to the Omnipresent; whoever is not pleasing to people is not pleasing to the Omnipresent.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas says: Morning sleep, midday wine, childish chatter, and sitting in the meeting places of the ignorant drive a person from the world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar of Modi’in says: One who profanes sacred things, disgraces the festivals, humiliates his fellow publicly, nullifies the covenant of Abraham our father, or interprets the Torah contrary to halakhah—even if he possesses Torah and good deeds—has no share in the World to Come.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yishmael says: Be yielding toward a superior, gentle with the young, and receive every person with joy.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Akiva says: Laughter and frivolity accustom a person to sexual immorality. Tradition is a fence for Torah; tithes are a fence for wealth; vows are a fence for abstinence; and silence is a fence for wisdom.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Beloved is the human being, for humanity was created in the image of God; an even greater love was made known in that humanity was created in the image, as it says: “For in the image of God He made humankind.” Beloved are Israel, for they are called children of the Omnipresent; an even greater love was made known in that they are called children, as it says: “You are children of the Lord your God.” Beloved are Israel, for a precious instrument was given to them; an even greater love was made known in that the precious instrument by which the world was created was given to them, as it says: “For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake My Torah.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given. The world is judged with goodness, and everything is according to the abundance of deeds.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Everything is given on collateral, and a net is spread over all living things. The shop is open, the shopkeeper gives credit, the ledger is open, the hand writes, and whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow. The collectors make their rounds continually every day and exact payment from a person with or without his awareness. They have what to rely upon; the judgment is a judgment of truth; and everything is prepared for the banquet.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says: If there is no Torah, there is no worldly conduct; if there is no worldly conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no reverence; if there is no reverence, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: One whose wisdom exceeds his deeds—what is he like? A tree with many branches and few roots; a wind comes, uproots it, and turns it over, as it says: “He shall be like a lonely shrub in the wilderness and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in parched places in the desert, a salt land uninhabited.” But one whose deeds exceed his wisdom—what is he like? A tree with few branches and many roots; even if all the winds in the world blow upon it, they do not move it from its place, as it says: “He shall be like a tree planted by water, sending out its roots by the stream. It does not fear when heat comes; its leaf remains fresh. In a year of drought it does not worry and never ceases to bear fruit.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma says: The laws of bird offerings and the beginnings of menstrual periods are essential bodies of halakhah; calculations of seasons and numerical values are appetizers to wisdom.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanania ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: “The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: All Israel has a share in the World to Come, as it is said: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever—the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take pride.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Chapter Four
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ben Zoma says: Who is wise? One who learns from every person, as it says: “From all my teachers I gained understanding.” Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination, as it says: “Better one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who captures a city.” Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion, as it says: “When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you and it is well with you”—happy in this world and well with you in the World to Come. Who is honored? One who honors others, as it says: “Those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me will be lightly esteemed.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ben Azzai says: Run to perform even a minor commandment as you would a major one, and flee from transgression; for one commandment leads to another commandment and one transgression leads to another. The reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Do not despise any person and do not dismiss any thing, for there is no person who does not have his hour and no thing that does not have its place.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says: Be exceedingly humble in spirit, for the end of mortal man is worms.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says: Whoever desecrates the Name of Heaven in secret is punished publicly. With regard to desecration of the Name, the unintentional and intentional are both held accountable.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yishmael his son says: One who studies in order to teach is enabled to study and to teach; one who studies in order to practice is enabled to study and teach, to observe and to practice.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Tzadok says: Do not separate yourself from the community; do not make yourself like legal advocates; do not make the Torah a crown with which to aggrandize yourself, nor a spade with which to dig. Thus Hillel said: one who makes use of the crown passes away. You learn from this that whoever derives personal benefit from words of Torah removes his life from the world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yose says: Whoever honors the Torah is himself honored by people; whoever dishonors the Torah is himself dishonored by people.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yishmael his son says: One who withholds himself from judging frees himself from enmity, theft, and a false oath; one who is arrogant in rendering rulings is foolish, wicked, and haughty.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Do not judge alone, for only One judges alone. And do not say, “Accept my opinion,” for they are entitled to decide, not you.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yonatan says: Whoever fulfills the Torah in poverty will ultimately fulfill it in wealth; whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will ultimately neglect it in poverty.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Meir says: Reduce your business activity and occupy yourself with Torah; be humble before every person. If you neglect Torah, many causes of idleness will confront you; if you labor in Torah, He has abundant reward to give you.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says: One who performs one commandment acquires one advocate; one who commits one transgression acquires one accuser. Repentance and good deeds are a shield against punishment.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yochanan the Sandalmaker says: Every gathering that is for the sake of Heaven will endure; one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not endure.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua says: Let the honor of your student be as dear to you as your own, the honor of your colleague as the reverence for your teacher, and the reverence for your teacher as the reverence of Heaven.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yehudah says: Be careful in study, for an error in study can amount to deliberate sin.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon says: There are three crowns—the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of kingship—but the crown of a good name rises above them all.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Nehorai says: Exile yourself to a place of Torah. Do not say that it will follow you, for your companions will establish it in your hand; and do not rely on your own understanding.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yannai says: It is not in our power to explain either the tranquility of the wicked or the sufferings of the righteous.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Matya ben Harash says: Be first to greet every person. Be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yaakov says: This world is like an entrance hall before the World to Come; prepare yourself in the entrance hall so that you may enter the banquet hall.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Better one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world than the entire life of the World to Come; and better one hour of spiritual delight in the World to Come than the entire life of this world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: Do not appease your fellow while he is angry; do not comfort him while his dead lies before him; do not question him at the moment of his vow; and do not seek to see him at the moment of his disgrace.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Shmuel HaKatan says: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice; when he stumbles, let not your heart be glad, lest the Lord see and it be displeasing in His eyes, and He turn His anger away from him.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Elisha ben Avuyah says: One who learns as a child—what is he like? Ink written on fresh paper. One who learns in old age—what is he like? Ink written on erased paper.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yose bar Yehudah of Kfar HaBavli says: One who learns from the young—what is he like? One who eats unripe grapes and drinks wine straight from the press. One who learns from the old—what is he like? One who eats ripe grapes and drinks aged wine.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Meir says: Do not look at the vessel but at what is inside it. There is a new vessel full of old wine, and an old vessel that does not even contain new wine.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: Jealousy, desire, and honor drive a person from the world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: Those born are destined to die, the dead to live again, and the living to be judged—to know, to make known, and to become known that He is God: He is the Maker, the Creator, the Knower, the Judge, the Witness, the Litigant, and He will judge. Blessed is He, before Whom there is no injustice, no forgetfulness, no favoritism, and no taking of bribes. Know that everything is according to the reckoning. Let not your inclination assure you that the grave is a refuge, for against your will you were formed, against your will you were born, against your will you live, against your will you die, and against your will you will give judgment and account before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanania ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: “The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: All Israel has a share in the World to Come, as it is said: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever—the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take pride.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Chapter Five
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: The world was created with ten utterances. Could it not have been created with one? Rather, this teaches the gravity of the wicked who destroy a world created with ten utterances, and the reward of the righteous who sustain a world created with ten utterances.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There were ten generations from Adam to Noah, showing how patient God is, for all those generations angered Him until He brought the waters of the Flood upon them. There were ten generations from Noah to Abraham, showing how patient God is, for all those generations angered Him until Abraham our father came and received the reward of them all.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Abraham our father was tested with ten trials and stood firm through them all, showing how great was Abraham our father’s love.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ten miracles were performed for our ancestors in Egypt and ten at the sea. The Holy One, blessed be He, brought ten plagues upon the Egyptians in Egypt and ten at the sea. Our ancestors tested the Holy One, blessed be He, ten times in the wilderness, as it says: “They tested Me these ten times and did not listen to My voice.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ten miracles were performed for our ancestors in the Temple: no woman miscarried from the smell of sacrificial meat; sacrificial meat never spoiled; no fly was seen in the slaughterhouse; no seminal emission occurred to the High Priest on Yom Kippur; rain never extinguished the altar fire; the wind never dispersed the pillar of smoke; no defect was found in the Omer, the Two Loaves, or the Showbread; the people stood crowded yet bowed with space; no snake or scorpion ever harmed anyone in Jerusalem; and no one said to another, “There is no room for me to lodge in Jerusalem.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ten things were created on the eve of the first Shabbat at twilight: the mouth of the earth, the mouth of the well, the mouth of the donkey, the rainbow, the manna, the staff, the shamir, the script, the writing, and the tablets. Some say also destructive spirits, the burial place of Moses, and the ram of Abraham our father; and some say also the first tongs, made with tongs.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Seven things characterize an unformed person and seven a wise person. A wise person does not speak before one greater in wisdom or number; does not interrupt another; is not hasty to answer; asks to the point and answers properly; addresses first things first and last things last; says “I have not heard” about what he has not heard; and admits the truth. The opposites characterize an unformed person.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Seven kinds of punishment come to the world for seven classes of transgression. When some tithe and some do not, a famine from drought comes: some are hungry and some have plenty. When all resolve not to tithe, a famine of turmoil and drought comes. When they also fail to separate challah, a famine of destruction comes. Pestilence comes for capital sins mentioned in the Torah that were not handed over to the court, and for misuse of Sabbatical-year produce. The sword comes for delayed justice, perverted justice, and those who rule in Torah contrary to halakhah.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Wild beasts come to the world because of false oaths and desecration of God’s Name. Exile comes because of idolatry, sexual immorality, bloodshed, and failure to observe the sabbatical year. Pestilence increases at four times: in the fourth year, the seventh, after the seventh, and after Sukkot each year—because of neglected gifts to the poor and misuse of Sabbatical produce.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four types of people: one who says “Mine is mine and yours is yours” is average; some say this is the trait of Sodom. “Mine is yours and yours is mine” is an ignorant person. “Mine is yours and yours is yours” is pious. “Mine is mine and yours is mine” is wicked.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four temperaments: easy to anger and easy to appease—his gain is canceled by his loss. Hard to anger and hard to appease—his loss is canceled by his gain.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: According to another reading the order is reversed. Hard to anger and easy to appease is pious; easy to anger and hard to appease is wicked.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four types of students: quick to understand and quick to forget—his gain is canceled by his loss; slow to understand and slow to forget—his loss is canceled by his gain; quick to understand and slow to forget—this is a good portion; slow to understand and quick to forget—this is a bad portion.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four types among those who give charity: one who wants to give but does not want others to give has an evil eye toward others; one who wants others to give but will not give himself has an evil eye toward himself; one who gives and wants others to give is pious; one who neither gives nor wants others to give is wicked.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four types among those who go to the study hall: one who goes but does not practice has the reward for going; one who practices but does not go has the reward for practice; one who goes and practices is pious; one who neither goes nor practices is wicked.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: There are four types among those who sit before sages: sponge, funnel, strainer, and sieve. The sponge absorbs everything. The funnel takes in at one end and lets out at the other. The strainer lets the wine pass and retains the sediment. The sieve lets the coarse flour pass and retains the fine flour.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Any love dependent on something ends when that thing ends. Love not dependent on anything never ends. What is love dependent on something? The love of Amnon and Tamar. What is love not dependent on anything? The love of David and Jonathan.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Any dispute for the sake of Heaven will endure; one not for the sake of Heaven will not endure. What is a dispute for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. What is one not for the sake of Heaven? The dispute of Korach and all his congregation.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Whoever brings merit to the many is not caused to sin; whoever causes the many to sin is not given sufficient opportunity to repent. Moses was meritorious and brought merit to the many, so their merit depends on him; Jeroboam sinned and caused the many to sin, so their sin depends on him.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Whoever has these three traits is among the disciples of Abraham our father: a good eye, a humble spirit, and a modest soul. Whoever has an evil eye, a haughty spirit, and a broad appetite is among the disciples of wicked Balaam. Abraham’s disciples enjoy this world and inherit the World to Come; Balaam’s disciples inherit Gehinnom and descend to the pit of destruction.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Yehudah ben Tema says: Be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and strong as a lion to do the will of your Father in Heaven.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: The brazen-faced are destined for Gehinnom and the shamefaced for the Garden of Eden. May it be Your will, Lord our God and God of our fathers, that the Temple be rebuilt speedily in our days, and grant us our share in Your Torah.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: He would say: At five years, Scripture; at ten, Mishnah; at thirteen, commandments; at fifteen, Talmud; at eighteen, marriage; at twenty, pursuit; at thirty, strength; at forty, understanding; at fifty, counsel; at sixty, old age; at seventy, gray hair; at eighty, special strength; at ninety, bending; at one hundred, as though dead, passed away, and removed from the world.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ben Bag Bag says: Turn it and turn it again, for everything is in it. Look deeply into it; grow old and worn in it; do not move away from it, for you have no better measure than it.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Ben He He says: According to the effort is the reward.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanania ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: “The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: All Israel has a share in the World to Come, as it is said: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever—the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take pride.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Chapter Six
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: The sages taught in the language of the Mishnah: Blessed is He Who chose them and their teaching.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Meir says: Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things; moreover, the entire world is worthwhile for his sake. He is called friend and beloved, one who loves the Omnipresent and loves people, gladdens the Omnipresent and gladdens people. Torah clothes him with humility and reverence, prepares him to be righteous, pious, upright, and faithful, distances him from sin and brings him near to merit. From him people benefit by counsel, sound wisdom, understanding, and strength. Torah gives him kingship, authority, and discernment in judgment; the secrets of Torah are revealed to him; he becomes like an ever-flowing spring and an unceasing river, modest, patient, and forgiving of insult; and it raises and exalts him above all deeds.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: Every day a heavenly voice goes out from Mount Horeb proclaiming: “Woe to the people for the insult to Torah!” Whoever does not engage in Torah is called rebuked. Scripture says: “A gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman without discretion,” and: “The tablets were the work of God and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.” Do not read harut, “engraved,” but herut, “freedom,” for no one is truly free except one who engages in Torah study. Whoever engages in Torah study becomes elevated, as it says: “From Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamot.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: One who learns from his fellow even one chapter, one law, one verse, one statement, or even one letter must treat him with honor. We find that David, king of Israel, learned only two things from Ahitophel and nevertheless called him his teacher, guide, and intimate. If David did so after learning only two things, how much more must one honor a fellow from whom he learns even one chapter, law, verse, statement, or letter. There is no honor except Torah, as it says: “The wise shall inherit honor,” and “The wholehearted shall inherit good.” There is no good except Torah, as it says: “For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake My Torah.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: This is the way of Torah: eat bread with salt, drink water in measure, sleep on the ground, live a life of hardship, and labor in Torah. If you do so, “happy are you and it is well with you”—happy in this world and well with you in the World to Come.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Do not seek greatness for yourself and do not crave honor. Do more than your learning. Do not desire the table of kings, for your table is greater than theirs and your crown greater than theirs; and your Employer is faithful to pay you the reward for your work.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Torah is greater than priesthood and kingship. Kingship is acquired through thirty qualities, priesthood through twenty-four, but Torah through forty-eight things: study, attentive listening, clear speech, understanding of the heart, awe, reverence, humility, joy, purity, serving sages, close association with colleagues, discussion with students, composure, Scripture, Mishnah, little business, little worldly occupation, little pleasure, little sleep, little conversation, little laughter, patience, a good heart, faith in the sages, acceptance of suffering, knowing one’s place, rejoicing in one’s portion, making a fence around one’s words, not taking credit for oneself, being loved, loving the Omnipresent, loving people, loving righteous deeds, loving uprightness, loving rebuke, keeping far from honor, not being arrogant in learning, not delighting in issuing rulings, sharing another’s burden, judging him favorably, establishing him in truth and peace, settling one’s heart in study, asking and answering, hearing and adding, learning in order to teach, learning in order to practice, making one’s teacher wiser, accurately preserving what one has heard, and saying something in the name of the one who said it. Whoever says a thing in the name of its speaker brings redemption to the world, as it says: “Esther told the king in Mordecai’s name.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Great is Torah, for it gives life to those who practice it in this world and in the World to Come, as Scripture says: “They are life to those who find them and healing to all their flesh”; “It shall be healing to your navel and marrow to your bones”; “It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it”; and many other verses promising grace, long life, wealth, honor, pleasant ways, and peace.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: Beauty, strength, wealth, honor, wisdom, old age, gray hair, and children are fitting for the righteous and fitting for the world. Scripture praises gray hair, wisdom, descendants, strength, and honor. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says: These qualities that the sages counted for the righteous were all fulfilled in Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi and his sons.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma said: Once I was walking on the road and a man greeted me. He asked where I came from, and I said from a great city of sages and scribes. He offered me enormous wealth if I would live in his town. I replied: Even if you gave me all the silver, gold, precious stones, and pearls in the world, I would live only in a place of Torah. When a person departs, neither silver nor gold nor precious stones accompany him, but only Torah and good deeds. Torah guides a person in this world, guards him in the grave, and speaks for him in the World to Come. Therefore “The Torah of Your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver,” and: “Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, says the Lord of Hosts.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: The Holy One, blessed be He, acquired five possessions in His world: Torah, heaven and earth, Abraham, Israel, and the Temple. Scripture speaks of each as His possession.
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world He created only for His glory, as it says: “Everyone who is called by My name, whom I created for My glory, whom I formed and made,” and: “The Lord shall reign forever and ever.”
paragraphs.note: Reviewed Pirkei Avot translation completed for Kavvanah Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Hanania ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments, as it is said: “The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to magnify Torah and make it glorious.”
paragraphs.note: Reused from an identical reviewed Hebrew paragraph elsewhere in the bundled Siddur.

paragraphs.text: Order of separating terumot and tithes.

Produce grown in the Land of Israel under Jewish ownership is subject to the obligations of terumot and tithes. Produce for which it is unknown whether these were separated is regarded as demai and requires separation without a blessing. When it is certain they were not separated, one separates with a blessing: recite the blessing before the separation, then pronounce the prescribed declaration.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Formula for separating priestly gifts and tithes from produce of doubtful untithed status (demai).
Take slightly more than one percent of the fruit, separate it from the rest, and say:

One hundredth of what is here shall remain untithed produce. The amount exceeding one hundredth at the north side is designated as the great terumah. [When separating tithes from multiple kinds, say: 'Each kind for its own kind.'] The one hundredth here, together with nine equal parts at the north side of the produce [each kind for its own kind], constitutes the first tithe. The one hundredth I designated as first tithe shall be the terumat ma'aser—the tithe contribution. [For multiple kinds, say: 'Each kind for its own kind.']
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: If a second tithe is required, let the produce on the south side be designated as the second tithe [when there is more than one kind: 'each kind for its own kind']. Let that tithe, together with its added fifth, be redeemed onto one perutah of the coin I designated for redemption. If a poor person's tithe is required, let it be designated on the south side of the produce [each kind for its own kind]. If there are fourth-year fruits here, let their sanctity, with the added fifth, be transferred to one perutah of the coin I designated for redemption.
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Formula for separating priestly gifts and tithes from produce certainly requiring tithes (tevel vadai).
If you grew the produce and know exactly when each fruit began to develop and when it was harvested, recite the formula with its blessing as follows:
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to separate priestly gifts and tithes.

One hundredth of the produce here shall remain untithed. The quantity greater than one hundredth on the north side is designated as the great terumah. [If there are several kinds, say: 'Each kind for its own kind.'] That one hundredth together with nine comparable parts on the north side [for multiple kinds: each kind for its own kind] shall be the first tithe. The one hundredth I designated as first tithe is made the terumat ma'aser, the contribution from that tithe. [For more than one kind, say: 'Each kind for its own kind.']
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Produce from the first, second, fourth, and fifth years of the sabbatical cycle requires the second tithe; therefore add the following formula:
The second tithe shall be on the south side of the produce. For more than one species, add: 'each species from its own kind.'
After separating the second tithe, redeem its sanctity onto a coin worth at least a perutah. Before redemption, recite:
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of the second tithe.
And recite the formula for transferring the produce's sacred status:
The second tithe here, together with its added fifth, shall be redeemed onto one perutah of the coin that I designated for this purpose.

Produce from the third and sixth years of the sabbatical cycle is exempt from the second tithe but subject to the poor tithe; no redemption is needed. Therefore, instead of the second-tithe separation and redemption, say:
The poor tithe shall be on the south side of the produce; for more than one species say: 'each species from its own kind.'
If the fruit is definitely neta revai (fourth-year produce) and you know it has not yet been redeemed, recite:
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of fourth-year produce.
And recite the formula for transferring the produce's sacred status:
The fourth-year produce here, together with its added fifth, shall be redeemed onto one perutah of the coin that I designated for this purpose.
Blessing on seeing a rainbow.
One who sees a rainbow should recite this blessing. Do not gaze at it; look only briefly in order to say the blessing.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who remembers the covenant, is faithful to His covenant, and fulfills His word.
Mishnah readings.
Mishnah Shabbat selections for the first meal.

Chapter 1. 1. The acts of carrying objects on Shabbat: there are two that amount to four for the person inside and two that amount to four for the person outside. For example, a poor man stands in the courtyard and a householder inside. If the poor man extends his hand inside and puts an object into the householder's hand, or takes one from the householder's hand and carries it outside, the poor man is liable to bring a sin offering and the householder is exempt. If the householder extends his hand outside and puts an object into the poor man's hand, or takes one from the poor man's hand and brings it in, the householder is liable and the poor man is exempt. If the poor man extends his hand inside and the householder takes an object from it, or the householder puts an object into the poor man's hand and the latter carries it outside, both are exempt. Likewise, if the householder extends his hand outside and the poor man takes an object from it, or places an object in it and the householder brings it inside, both are exempt. 2. One must not sit down for a haircut immediately before the time of Minchah until one has prayed. One must not enter the bathhouse, a tannery, sit down to eat or begin legal proceedings. If they have already begun, they need not interrupt them. One interrupts for the recital of the Shema, but not for the Amidah prayer. 3. A tailor must not go out with his needle as dusk approaches, lest he forget and carry it on Shabbat; nor may a scribe go out with his pen. One must not search clothing for parasites or read by lamplight. A teacher may watch where children are reading, but must not read himself. Likewise, a man with a ritual discharge must not eat together with a woman in a state of ritual impurity, lest they become accustomed to transgression. 4. These are the decrees enacted in the upper chamber of Hananiah son of Hezekiah son of Gurion when the sages came to visit him. The disciples of the school of Shammai outnumbered those of the school of Hillel, and on that day eighteen restrictions were enacted. 5. The school of Shammai says: one must not soak ink, dyes or fodder beans on the eve of Shabbat unless they will become soaked before dark. The school of Hillel permits it. 6. According to the school of Shammai, one must not put flax in an oven to steam unless it will finish before nightfall, nor wool into a dyeing vat unless it will absorb the dye in time. The school of Hillel permits both. According to the school of Shammai, one must not set traps for beasts, birds or fish unless they will catch their prey before dark. The school of Hillel permits it. 7. The school of Shammai forbids selling merchandise to a non-Jew, loading together with him or giving him a burden before Shabbat unless he can reach a nearby place before dark. The school of Hillel permits it. 8. The school of Shammai forbids delivering hides to a tanner or clothes to a non-Jewish launderer unless the work will be finished before dark. The school of Hillel permits all these things until sunset. 9. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: in my father's household it was customary to give white linen to a non-Jewish launderer three days before Shabbat. Both schools agree that an olive press and a wine press may be tightened beforehand. 10. Meat, onions and eggs may be roasted before Shabbat only if they will be roasted by nightfall. Bread may be placed in an oven and a cake upon the coals only if a crust will form in time. Rabbi Eliezer says it suffices for the lower crust to form. 11. The Paschal offering may be lowered into the oven before nightfall, and a fire may be lit in the Temple's hearth chamber. Outside the Temple, a fire must take hold of most of the wood before dark; Rabbi Yehudah says that with charcoal it is sufficient for combustion merely to begin.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text:
1. With what may lamps be lit, and with what may they not be lit? They may not be lit with cedar bast, uncombed flax, silk waste, willow fiber, desert fiber, or the green growth on the surface of water; nor with pitch, wax, castor oil, oil of consecrated produce that must be burned, tail fat, or ordinary fat. Nahum the Mede says: they may be lit with rendered fat. The Sages say: whether rendered or not, it may not be used.
2. On a festival one may not light with oil of consecrated produce that must be burned. Rabbi Yishmael says: one may not light with tar out of respect for the Sabbath. The Sages permit all oils: sesame oil, nut oil, radish-seed oil, fish oil, gourd oil, tar, and naphtha. Rabbi Tarfon says: only olive oil may be used.
3. Of materials that grow from a tree, none may be used as a wick except flax; and of such materials none contracts impurity through a tent except flax. A cloth wick that was folded but not singed: Rabbi Eliezer says it is impure and may not be lit; Rabbi Akiva says it is pure and may be lit.
4. A person may not pierce an eggshell, fill it with oil, and place it above the mouth of a lamp so that it drips into it, even if the vessel is earthenware; Rabbi Yehudah permits it. But if a potter joined it to the lamp from the outset, it is permitted because it is one vessel. A person may not fill a bowl with oil, set it beside the lamp, and put the end of the wick into it so that it draws oil; Rabbi Yehudah permits it.
5. One who extinguishes a lamp because of fear of non-Jews, robbers, or an evil spirit, or for a sick person so that he may sleep, is exempt. If he does so to save the lamp, the oil, or the wick, he is liable. Rabbi Yose exempts in all these cases except the wick, because he makes it into charcoal.
6. For three transgressions women die in childbirth: for not being careful regarding the laws of niddah, separating challah, and lighting the Sabbath lamp.
7. Three things a person must say in the home on Friday evening as darkness approaches: “Have you tithed? Have you made the eruv? Light the lamp!” At twilight, when it is uncertain whether darkness has fallen, one may not tithe produce certainly untithed, immerse vessels, or light lamps; but one may tithe demai, establish an eruv, and insulate hot food.
paragraphs.note: Previously translated paragraph, Hebrew similarity 98.4%: source and target independently present in source corpus.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 3. 1. Food may be left on a stove fired with straw or stubble. If it was fired with olive press waste or wood, it is prohibited until the coals are removed or covered with ashes. The school of Shammai permits leaving hot water, but not food; the school of Hillel permits both water and food. The school of Shammai permits removing a vessel but not returning it; the school of Hillel permits returning it as well. 2. An oven, even if fired with straw or stubble, may not have a pot set inside it or upon it. A small stove called a kupach, if fired with straw or stubble, is treated like a cooking stove; if fired with wood or press waste, it is treated like an oven. 3. One must not put an egg beside a kettle to cook it or wrap it in hot cloths; Rabbi Yose permits the latter. One must not bury an egg in heated sand or the dust of a road in order to roast it. 4. The people of Tiberias led cold water through a pipe passing through the hot springs. The sages said: on Shabbat that water is like water heated on Shabbat and may neither be used for washing nor drunk. On a festival it is like water heated on a festival: it may not be used for washing but may be drunk. One may drink on Shabbat from a mulyar kettle whose coals have been removed, but not from an antikhi vessel even when its coals are removed. 5. One must not pour cold water into an emptied hot kettle to heat it, but enough may be poured in that it will only become lukewarm, whether into a kettle or into a cup. One must not put spices into a boiling pan or pot that has just been taken from the fire; one may put them into a bowl or plate. Rabbi Yehudah permits adding them anywhere except to a dish containing vinegar or fish brine. 6. One must not set a vessel beneath a lamp to collect dripping oil. If one placed it there before Shabbat, it is permitted; but the collected oil may not be used because it was not prepared for use. A new lamp may be moved, an old one may not. Rabbi Shimon permits moving all lamps except one that was burning on Shabbat. One may put a vessel beneath a lamp to catch sparks but may not put water in it to extinguish them.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 4. 1. With what may a vessel of hot food be insulated to retain heat, and with what may it not? It may not be insulated with pressed olive refuse, manure, salt, lime or sand, whether wet or dry. It may not be insulated with damp straw, grape skins, flax tow or herbs, but these may be used when dry. It may be insulated with clothing, produce, pigeons' wings, carpenter's sawdust or fine flax tow. Rabbi Judah prohibits fine tow but permits coarse tow. 2. Hides may be used for insulating and may be moved. Wool may be used for insulating but may not be moved. What should one do? Remove the lid and let the wool fall by itself. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says that the basket must be tilted to the side and the vessel taken out; otherwise, after taking it out one may be unable to put it back. The Sages say it may be removed and returned. A vessel that was not insulated before nightfall may not be insulated after Shabbat begins. If it had been insulated and then became uncovered, it may be covered again. One may fill a jug with water and place it under a pillow or beneath the headrest.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 4, complete working translation checked against the bundled Hebrew and Russian.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 5. 1. With what gear may an animal go out on Shabbat? A camel with a halter; a female camel with a nose bridle; a Libyan donkey with a bridle; and a horse with a collar. Animals accustomed to a collar may go out and be led by it; the harness may be sprinkled with purification water and immersed in a mikveh without being removed. 2. A donkey may go out with a securely fastened blanket, rams with leather chest coverings, sheep with their tails bound, their legs tied or with protective bands, and goats with their udders bound. Rabbi Yose forbids all these except the sheep's protective bands. Rabbi Yehudah permits binding the udders of goats to stop milk production but not to collect the milk. 3. A camel may not go out with a weight tied on, or with its forelegs or hindlegs bound together; the same applies to other animals. One must not tie camels together and lead them in a chain. One may hold their ropes in one's hand, but may not wind them around it. 4. A donkey may not go out with an unsecured blanket, a bell even if plugged, a wooden ladder on its neck or a strap on its leg. Roosters may not go out with threads or straps on their legs; rams may not go out with a cart beneath the tail, sheep with scented protective substances, calves with a yoke, or cows with a hedgehog skin or a strap between the horns. The cow of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah went out with a strap between its horns, but the sages did not approve.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 6. 1. With which adornments may a woman go out, and with which may she not? She may not go out with woolen or linen threads or ribbons in her hair; nor may she immerse with them in a mikveh until she loosens them. She may not go out with a forehead ornament called a totefet or with pendants unless they are sewn on, with a head ornament called a kavul into a public domain, with a golden crown in the form of a city, a necklace, earrings, a ring without a seal or a needle without an eye. If she did go out, she is not liable to bring a sin offering. 2. A man may not go out in a sandal studded with nails, wearing one sandal when the other foot has no wound, with tefillin, with an amulet from an unrecognized healer, a breastplate, helmet or greaves. If he went out, he is not liable to bring a sin offering. 3. A woman may not go out with a needle having an eye, a ring with a seal, a neck pin, a pouch of spices or a flask of balsam. If she goes out, she is liable to bring a sin offering, according to Rabbi Meir; the sages exempt her for the spice pouch and balsam flask. 4. A man may not go out with a sword, bow, shield, club or spear. If he does, he is liable to bring a sin offering. Rabbi Eliezer considers these ornaments, but the sages call them a disgrace, as it is said: 'They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.' A strap on the leg is ritually pure and may be worn outside; chains are impure and may not be worn outside. 5. A woman may go out with threads of hair, whether her own, another person's, or animal hair; with a totefet or pendants if they are sewn on; in a courtyard, with a kavul or a wig; with cotton in her ear, her shoe or for personal hygiene; and with a peppercorn, a grain of salt or another object in her mouth if she placed it there before Shabbat. If it falls out, she may not put it back. Rabbi permits going out with an artificial or gold tooth, but the sages forbid it. 6. One may go out with a coin placed against a wound on the foot. Girls may go out with threads or even little wooden sticks in their ears. Arabian women may go out with their faces veiled and Median women with their cloaks fastened; these practices are permitted to everyone, the sages having merely described common custom. 7. Clothing may be fastened with a stone, nut or coin, but one must not make a new fastener on Shabbat. 8. According to Rabbi Meir, a person with an amputated leg may go out with a wooden prosthesis; Rabbi Yose forbids it. If the prosthesis has a recess for padding it can contract ritual impurity. Supports used for moving about contract impurity by being sat upon; one may go out with them on Shabbat and enter the Temple courtyard with them. A seat and its supports contract impurity through sitting; one may neither go out with them on Shabbat nor enter the Temple courtyard with them. Stilts are ritually pure, but may not be taken outside. 9. Children may go out with protective knots and royal children with bells; everyone is permitted to do so, the sages having described typical practice. 10. Rabbi Meir permits going out for healing with a locust egg, a fox's tooth or a nail from a crucified person. The sages say that even on weekdays this is forbidden as a pagan practice.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 7. 1. A fundamental rule concerning Shabbat: someone who entirely forgot the existence of Shabbat and worked on many Sabbaths brings only one sin offering. Someone who knows about Shabbat but mistakenly violates its prohibitions over many Sabbaths incurs separate liability for each Sabbath. Someone who knows today is Shabbat yet performs many kinds of forbidden labor is liable for each separate principal category of labor. For several derivative acts of one category only one sin offering is brought. 2. There are thirty-nine principal kinds of forbidden labor: sowing, plowing, reaping, binding sheaves, threshing, winnowing, selecting, grinding, sifting, kneading and baking; shearing wool, bleaching, combing, dyeing, spinning, stretching the warp, forming two loops of the loom, weaving two threads and unraveling two threads; tying and untying knots, sewing two stitches and tearing in order to sew two stitches; trapping a deer, slaughtering it, flaying it, salting, curing, scraping and cutting its hide; writing two letters and erasing in order to write two letters; building and demolishing, extinguishing and kindling fire, striking the final hammer blow, and transferring an article from one domain to another. These are the thirty-nine principal categories. 3. Another rule: one who carries on Shabbat an object that people normally store and that is fit for storage is liable. If an object is not normally stored and is unfit for storage, only the person who set it aside for a specific purpose is liable. 4. The minimum amount of straw carried is what fills a cow's mouth; bean husks, a camel's mouth; stalks, a lamb's mouth; grass, a kid's mouth; fresh garlic or onion leaves, the volume of a dried fig; dry leaves, a kid's mouth. Different kinds are not combined because their measures differ. The minimum quantity of food is the volume of a dried fig. Food items can be combined because they share one measure, not counting their peels, seeds, stems, bran or grain husks. Rabbi Judah excepts lentil husks, since they are cooked together with the lentils.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 7, source-aligned full working English translation.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 8. 1. The minimum quantity of wine carried is enough to dilute a cup; of milk, one swallow; of honey, enough to put on a wound; of oil, enough to anoint the smallest joint; of water, enough to moisten a healing eye dressing; of other drinks and wastewater, a quarter-log. Rabbi Shimon says a quarter-log applies to them all; the smaller measures apply only to someone who set those substances aside for a special purpose. 2. The minimum quantity of rope is enough to make a handle for a basket; of reed, enough to repair a sieve or strainer. Rabbi Yehudah says: enough to measure a child's shoe. Of paper: enough to write a customs receipt; one who carries the receipt itself is likewise liable. Of erased paper: enough to wrap around the mouth of a small perfume flask. 3. Of leather: enough to make an amulet; of parchment, enough to write the shortest passage of the tefillin, 'Hear, O Israel'; of ink, enough to write two letters; of black eye cosmetic, enough for one eye. 4. Of glue: enough for the tip of a bird-catching rod; of pitch and sulfur: enough to seal a hole; of wax: enough to close a small opening; of clay: enough for the mouth of a goldsmith's furnace (Rabbi Yehudah: enough to make a small support); of bran: enough to cover the furnace opening; of lime: enough to anoint the face of a young girl (Rabbi Yehudah: enough to make a pattern; Rabbi Nehemiah: enough to make a thin mask). 5. Of earth: according to Rabbi Akiva enough to seal large packages, but according to the sages enough to seal letters. Of dung or fine sand: according to Rabbi Akiva enough to fertilize one cabbage stalk, and according to the sages one leek; of coarse sand, enough for a full spoonful of lime; of reed, enough to make a pen. If the reed is thick or damaged, enough to cook the lightest egg, beaten in a frying pan, upon it. 6. Of bone: enough to make a spoon, though Rabbi Yehudah says enough for a tooth; of glass: enough to sharpen the tip of a weaver's shuttle; of stone: enough to throw at a bird, or according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, at an animal. 7. Of a potsherd: according to Rabbi Yehudah, enough to place between logs; Rabbi Meir says enough to rake out coals; Rabbi Yose says enough to hold a quarter-log. Rabbi Meir cited the verse, 'No potsherd will be found among its fragments to take fire.' Rabbi Yose answered that the same verse continues, 'or to scoop up water from a cistern.'
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Weekday morning prayer.
Petichat Eliyahu (Elijah's Opening).
It is customary to recite Petichat Eliyahu before prayer, as it is traditionally believed to help prayer be accepted and open the heart.
May the favor of the LORD our God be upon us; establish the work of our hands for us—yes, establish the work of our hands.

Elijah the prophet, may his memory be for good, began and said: Master of the worlds! You are One, but not a unit that can be counted. You are higher than all the exalted and more concealed than anything hidden; no thought can grasp You at all. You brought forth ten arrangements, which we call the ten sefirot, to govern through them the concealed worlds that are not revealed and the revealed worlds. Through them You are hidden from human beings. You bind them together and unite them. And because You are within them, whoever separates one of these ten from the others is considered as though he caused a division in You Yourself.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: These ten sefirot proceed in their order: one long, another short, and a third intermediate. You govern them, but no one governs You, neither from above nor below nor from any direction. You fashioned garments for them, from which human souls emerge, and many bodies which are called bodies relative to the garments that cover them. In this arrangement their names are: Hesed, the right arm; Gevurah, the left arm; Tiferet, the torso; Netzah and Hod, the two legs; Yesod, the completion of the body and the sign of the holy covenant; Malkhut, the mouth, called the Oral Torah. Hokhmah is the brain, the hidden thought; Binah is the heart, and through the heart one understands. Concerning these two it is written, 'The hidden things belong to the Lord our God.' The supernal Keter is the royal crown, of which it is said, 'He declares the end from the beginning.' It is the head tefillin. Within it is the holy name Yod–Heh–Vav–Heh, the path of emanation. It is the life-giving moisture of the tree, nourishing its limbs and branches like water with which a tree is watered and by which it grows.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Master of the worlds! You are the cause of all causes and the foundation of all foundations. You nourish the tree through that spring, and that spring is to the tree as a soul is to a body, giving it life. No likeness or image can represent You, among things within or without. You created heaven and earth, and brought forth from them the sun, the moon, the stars and constellations; upon earth You brought forth trees and plants, the Garden of Eden and herbs, beasts, birds, fish and human beings, so that through them the upper worlds might be known, how both above and below are governed through them, and how these powers are revealed through them. But no one can grasp You Yourself. Apart from You there is no unity above or below; You are acknowledged as Master over all. Each sefirah has a particular name, and by these names the angels are called; but You have no particular name, for You fill all names and are their perfection. When You withdraw from them, all the names remain like a body without a soul. You are wise, but not with the wisdom we know; You understand, but not with the understanding familiar to us. No place can define You; only Your strength and power are disclosed to human beings, showing how the world is governed by judgment and mercy, righteousness and justice, according to human deeds. Judgment is Gevurah; justice is the middle pillar; righteousness is holy Malkhut; the true scales are the two pillars of truth; the true measure is the sign of the covenant. All these reveal the governance of the world, but none means that You are limited by a particular righteousness called judgment, a particular justice called mercy, or by any of those qualities. Arise, Rabbi Shimon, and let words be renewed through you: you have been given permission to reveal hidden mysteries which until now no human being has been permitted to disclose.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon arose, began, and said: 'Yours, Lord, are greatness and power...' Listen, dwellers of the upper worlds! You who sleep in Hebron, and you, faithful shepherd, wake from your slumber! 'Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust!' These are the righteous of whom it is said: 'I sleep, but my heart is awake.' They are not dead, and for this reason they are told to awaken and sing. Faithful shepherd, arise with the patriarchs and sing to awaken the Divine Presence sleeping in exile, for until now all the righteous have been as sleepers with closed eyes. Then the Shekhinah spoke three times to the faithful shepherd and said: 'Rise up, faithful shepherd, for of you it is said, The voice of my beloved knocks, with the four letters of His name. And He says: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for Your punishment has ended, daughter of Zion, and He will no longer carry you into exile.' 'My head is covered with dew.' What is this dew? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'Do you imagine that since the Temple was destroyed I have returned to My house and entered My dwelling? No, I have not returned while you are in exile. Here is the sign: My head is filled with dew.' The letter heh signifies the Shekhinah in exile. Its perfection and life are expressed through the word tal, 'dew,' whose numerical value is thirty-nine. These are the letters Yod, Heh, and Vav, whereas the final Heh, the Shekhinah, is not counted in that number. Yod, Heh and Vav together equal thirty-nine, and this dew fills the Shekhinah with a stream from the source of all heavenly springs. Immediately the faithful shepherd rose with the holy patriarchs. To this point is the mystery of unity. Blessed be the Lord forever! Amen and amen.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: And Hannah prayed.

And Hannah prayed, and said: My heart exulteth in the LORD, My horn is exalted in the LORD; My mouth is enlarged over mine enemies; Because I rejoice in Thy salvation. There is none holy as the LORD, For there is none beside Thee; Neither is there any rock like our God. Multiply not exceeding proud talk; Let not arrogancy come out of your mouth; For the LORD is a God of knowledge, And by Him actions are weighed. The bows of the mighty men are broken, And they that stumbled are girded with strength. They that were full have hired out themselves for bread; And they that were hungry have ceased; While the barren hath borne seven, She that had many children hath languished. The LORD killeth, and maketh alive; He bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up. The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich; He bringeth low, He also lifteth up. . He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, He lifteth up the needy from the dung-hill, To make them sit with princes, And inherit the throne of glory; For the pillars of the earth are the LORD’S, And He hath set the world upon them. He will keep the feet of His holy ones, But the wicked shall be put to silence in darkness; For not by strength shall man prevail. They that strive with the LORD shall be broken to pieces; Against them will He thunder in heaven; The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; And He will give strength unto His king, And exalt the horn of His anointed. How great are His signs, and how mighty are His wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and His dominion from generation to generation. We are Your people and the flock of Your pasture; we will give thanks to You for ever, and declare Your praise from generation to generation. Evening, morning, and noon I pray and moan, and He hears my voice. When the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy. I will not fear ten thousands of people who have set themselves against me round about. As for me, I will look to the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.
