[On Shabbat and a festival omit the following verse:] Rejoice not against me, my enemy: though I have fallen, I shall arise; though I sit in darkness, the Lord is a light to me. For You, Lord, I wait; You will answer, Lord my God. My foot stands in an even place; in the assemblies I will bless the Lord.
paragraphs.note: Includes JPS 1917 public-domain biblical readings with translated liturgical additions; specialist proofread pending.

paragraphs.text: Zohar readings for the first Shabbat meal.
It is good to recite this passage of the Zohar concerning the honor of Shabbat (Yitro, folio 88a).

“Remember the Sabbath day, to sanctify it.” Rabbi Yitzchak said: It is written, “God blessed the seventh day,” yet concerning the manna it is written, “Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there shall be none.” Since food was not found on that day, where was the blessing to be found?

Rather, this is what was taught: all blessings, above and below, depend upon the seventh day. Why, then, is no manna found on the seventh day? Because from that day all six higher days receive blessing. Each gives sustenance to those below on its own day, drawing upon the blessing with which they were blessed on the seventh day.

For this reason, one who is on the level of faith should set the table and prepare a meal on Friday night, so that the table may be blessed throughout the six days. At that time blessing is made ready for the six weekdays, and blessing does not rest upon an empty table. Therefore one should prepare the Shabbat-night table with bread and food.

Rabbi Yitzchak said: Even during the day of Shabbat. Rabbi Yehudah said: A person should delight in this day and eat three meals on Shabbat, so that satisfaction and delight may be present in the world on that day.

Rabbi Abba said: This is to bring blessing to the upper days, which are blessed from this day. The day fills the head of Zeir Anpin with dew descending from the Holy Ancient One, hidden beyond all, and casts it upon the Field of Holy Apples three times from the entrance of Shabbat, so that all may be blessed together.

Therefore a person should delight at these three times, for the faith above depends upon them: upon the Holy Ancient One, Zeir Anpin, and the Field of Apples. A person should delight and rejoice in them. Whoever neglects one of these meals displays a blemish above, and that person’s punishment is severe.

For this reason one should set the table three times once Shabbat has begun. The table must not be found empty, so that blessing may rest upon it throughout the other days of the week. By this action a person demonstrates and attaches faith above.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Shimon said: Whoever completes the three Shabbat meals, a voice goes forth and proclaims about him: 'Then shall you delight in the LORD'—this is the first meal, corresponding to the Holy Ancient One, holiest of all; 'and I shall make you ride upon the heights of the earth'—this is the second meal, corresponding to the Field of Holy Apples; 'and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father'—this is the completion attained through Zeir Anpin.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Corresponding to these three meals a person should bring each meal to completion, delight in all of them and rejoice in each one, for in them is contained perfect faith. Therefore Shabbat is honored above all other appointed times and festivals: it contains everything that is not found in any other festival. Rabbi Hiyya said: 'Since everything is included in it, the seventh day is mentioned three times, as it is written: God completed on the seventh day; He rested on the seventh day; and God blessed the seventh day.'
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: When Rabbi Abba sat at a Shabbat meal, he rejoiced at every one. He would say: 'This is the holy meal of the Holy Ancient One, hidden from all.' At the other meal he would say: 'This is the meal of the Holy One, blessed be He.' Thus at each of the meals he rejoiced. When he had completed them, he said: 'The meals of faith have been completed.'
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: When Rabbi Shimon came to a meal, he would say: 'Prepare the meal of supreme faith; prepare the meal of the King,' then sit and rejoice. When he completed the third meal, a proclamation was made over him: 'Then shall you delight in the LORD, and I shall make you ride upon the heights of the earth, and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father.'
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Rabbi Elazar asked his father: 'How should these meals be arranged?' He answered: 'Concerning Shabbat night it is written, "I will cause you to ride upon the heights of the earth." On this night the Queen and the entire holy Apple Orchard are blessed; a person's table is blessed and an additional soul is bestowed. This night is the joy of the Queen. Therefore a person should rejoice in her joy and eat the Queen's meal.' 'Blessed be the Lord forever. Amen and amen.'
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: The Mishnah readings for the first meal appear at the end of the Siddur.
Blessings for the Haftarah.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who chose worthy prophets and delighted in their words, spoken in truth.
Blessed are You, LORD, who chose the Torah and Moses His servant, and Israel His people, and the prophets of truth and righteousness.
Read the Haftarah; the congregation reads it quietly. After the reading, say:
Our Redeemer—the LORD of Hosts is His name, the Holy One of Israel.
And then recite the blessing.

Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, Rock of all worlds, righteous in every generation, the faithful God who speaks and fulfills, promises and establishes, for all His words are true and just. You are faithful, LORD our God, and Your words are faithful: not one word of Yours shall return unfulfilled, for You are a faithful and merciful God and King. Blessed are You, LORD, the God faithful in all His words.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Have mercy upon Zion, for she is the house of our life, and swiftly save her downcast soul in our days. Blessed are You, LORD, who brings joy to Zion through her children.

Gladden us, LORD our God, with Elijah Your servant the prophet, and with the kingdom of the House of David, Your anointed one. May he come speedily and rejoice our hearts. No stranger shall sit on his throne, and others shall no longer inherit his honor, for You swore to him by Your holy name that his lamp shall never go out. Blessed are You, LORD, Shield of David.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: For the Torah, for the Temple service, for the Prophets and for this Shabbat day which You gave us, LORD our God, for holiness and rest, honor and glory: for everything, LORD our God, we thank You and bless You. May Your name be blessed by every living mouth forever. Blessed are You, LORD, who sanctifies Shabbat. Amen.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Announcement of Rosh Chodesh.

On the Shabbat preceding a New Moon, including the New Moon of Av, announce the New Moon and say 'May it be Your will,' except before the New Moon of Tishrei, which is not announced, as it is written: 'At the covered time, on our festival day.' It is proper to know the moment of the new moon; therefore some announce its exact time while reciting 'May it be Your will.'
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May it be the will of the God of heaven to establish the House of our life and swiftly return His Presence to it in our days. And say: Amen.
May it be the will of the God of heaven to show mercy to our remnant and halt plague, destruction, sword, famine, captivity and plunder from us and from His people Israel; and say: Amen.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May it be the will of the God of heaven to preserve all the sages of Israel, with their wives, children and students, wherever they dwell; and say: Amen.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May it be the will of the God of heaven that we hear good tidings, tidings of salvation and consolation, from the four corners of the earth. And say: Amen.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May He who performed miracles for our ancestors and redeemed them from Egypt redeem us and return the children to their borders. As a good omen for us, may Rosh Chodesh [month name] fall on [day or days; give the day of the new moon and the day on which it is observed]. May the Holy One, blessed be He, renew it for us and for His people Israel wherever they dwell, for good and blessing, gladness and joy, deliverance and consolation, livelihood and good sustenance, good news and favorable tidings; [in winter: for rain at its proper time; in summer: for dews of blessing], for complete healing and for redemption soon. And say: Amen.
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Announcement of a fast.

On the Shabbat before the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the Tenth of Tevet, the cantor announces the fast. The Ninth of Av, Yom Kippur, and the Fast of Esther are not announced; the Hebrew mnemonic is “AKaF.”

Brothers and sisters of the house of Israel, listen: the fast of the fourth month [the seventeenth of Tammuz], or the fast of the tenth month [the tenth of Tevet], will fall on [day]. May the Holy One, blessed be He, turn it into rejoicing and joy, as it is written: 'Thus says the Lord of Hosts: The fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and cheerful festivals; therefore love truth and peace.'
paragraphs.note: Original English working translation aligned to the full Hebrew paragraph; specialist review pending.

paragraphs.text: Reading of the Megillah.
Before the Megillah reading, the prayer leader recites the blessing while standing; the congregation also stands for the blessing.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to read the Megillah.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who performed miracles for our ancestors in those days, at this season.
On Purim night, when reciting Shehecheyanu for the first reading, intend that this blessing also cover the Purim meal and the sending of food gifts.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season.
Read the Megillah.
After the Megillah reading, roll up the scroll and then recite the blessing:

Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, [God] who fights our battle, judges our cause, avenges us, requites all the enemies of our lives and exacts payment from our oppressors. Blessed are You, LORD, who exacts retribution for His people Israel from all their oppressors, the God who saves.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Afterwards, say:
Cursed is Haman; blessed is Mordechai.
Cursed is Zeresh; blessed is Esther.
Cursed be all the wicked, blessed be all Israel, and may Harbonah also be remembered for good. Repeat three times.

Recite 'And You are holy,' and the cantor recites Kaddish Titkabbal. (Some also add 'A Song of Ascents of David: Had the LORD not been with us...' and then 'A Song of Ascents: I lift up my eyes...'). Recite Kaddish Yehei Shelama, Barekhu and Aleinu LeShabeach.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Order of Purim observances.

On Purim day, pray as on any weekday, adding Al HaNissim to the thanksgiving blessing. After the Amidah, recite Half Kaddish and take out the Torah scroll. Three people are called to the portion in Beshalach; the last verse is customarily repeated to complete ten verses.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said unto Joshua: ‘Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand.’ So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed; and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses’hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword. And the LORD said unto Moses: ‘Write this for a memorial in the book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.’ And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it Adonai-nissi. And he said: ‘The hand upon the throne of the LORD: the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.’
paragraphs.note: Public-domain JPS 1917 English aligned with the original Hebrew; any liturgical instructions are supplied by the project.

paragraphs.text: The cantor recites Half Kaddish, Ashrei and Uva LeTzion up to 'from now and forever.' The Megillah is read with blessings before and after it. After the reading, say 'And You are holy,' Kaddish Titkabbal and Yehalelu; return the Torah scroll to its place, then recite Beit Yaakov, the Song of the Day, Hoshienu, 'For the director of music, upon Ayyelet HaShachar,' Kaddish Yehei Shelama, and complete the service as on other days.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Third Shabbat meal.

Prepare the meal of perfect faith, the joy of the Holy King. Prepare the King’s meal: this is the meal of the holy King, the Radiant Countenance (with the Holy Ancient One and the field of holy apples coming to dine with Him).
Hymn for the afternoon meal, composed by Rabbi Isaac Luria, of blessed memory; tune: “O God of My Praise and Strength.”
Children of the palace who long to behold the radiance of Zeir Anpin,
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: be present at this table, where the King is inscribed in sacred forms.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Rejoice together at this gathering among the wakeful ones and all winged beings.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Rejoice now at this hour of favor, when there is no anger.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Draw close to me and behold my strength, for harsh judgments have no power here.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Outside they remain and do not enter, those insolent dogs.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Behold, I invite the Ancient of Days to behold Him until they have passed away.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: His revealed favor is to nullify every husk of impurity.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: He shall cast them into their holes, and they shall hide among the rocks.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: For now, at the afternoon offering, is the joy of Zeir Anpin.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Before the third Shabbat meal, one should say:

For the sake of the unity of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Presence, in awe and love and in love and awe, to unite the letters Yod–Heh with Vav–Heh in perfect unity, in the name of all Israel: I now come to fulfill the mitzvah of the third meal of Shabbat, corresponding to our father Jacob, the father of seventy souls. Through his merit may we be delivered from the war of Gog and Magog, and may the verse be fulfilled in us: 'I will feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father,' an inheritance without bounds. Through the virtue of these three meals, may we rectify the blemishes caused by optional feasts and forbidden foods. May the favor of the Lord our God be upon us; establish the work of our hands for us; establish the work of our hands.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Afterward, recite the passage from the holy Zohar that speaks of the honor of this meal.

Come and see: on all six weekdays, when the hour of Minhah prayer arrives, severe judgment rules and every judgment awakens. But on Shabbat, when the hour of Minhah comes, the Favor of all favors is disclosed and the Holy Ancient One reveals His will. Every decree is subdued and favor and joy prevail everywhere. It was precisely at this hour of favor that Moses, the faithful holy prophet, departed this world, so that all should know he did not depart under the power of judgment. At that hour his soul went forth through the favor of the Holy Ancient One and was concealed in Him. Hence it is said: 'No one knows the place of his burial.' Just as the Holy Ancient One is the most Hidden of all hidden things and is grasped by neither upper nor lower worlds, so this soul is hidden within the favor revealed at Shabbat Minhah. For that reason Scripture says: 'No one knows the place of his burial.' Moses is hidden beyond all else hidden in the world, and judgment has no power over him. Happy is Moses' portion! It has been taught: on this day the Torah is crowned with all its crowns—all its commandments, decrees and punishments—and with seventy branches of light shining in every direction. Who has seen the branches that spring from each branch? Five supports stand inside the tree, and all its branches rest upon them. Who has seen the gates opening in every direction? They all flash and shine with an unfailing light. A herald's voice calls: 'Awaken, holy ones in the upper worlds! Awake, holy people chosen above and below! Stir up joy before your Master; awaken to complete rejoicing. Prepare for the three joys of the three patriarchs, appear before faith, the joy of all joys. Happy is your portion, holy Israel, in this world and in the world to come! This is your inheritance among all the nations that worship idols.' Of this it is written: 'Between Me and the children of Israel.' Rabbi Judah said, 'It is indeed so.' Hence it is written: 'Remember the Sabbath day to make it holy.' And again: 'Be holy, for I the Lord am holy,' and 'You shall call the Sabbath a delight, the holy day of the Lord honorable.' It has been taught: on this day the souls of the righteous enjoy the mercies of the Holy Ancient One, the most Concealed of all. One spirit of delight from the Ancient One spreads through all the worlds, ascends, descends, and extends over all the holy children, over every keeper of Torah. They rest in complete rest and forget anger, judgment and hard labor, as it is said: 'On the day when the Lord gives you rest from your pain and your fear and the harsh bondage in which you served.' Therefore Shabbat is reckoned equal to the entire Torah, and one who keeps Shabbat is as though he kept the whole Torah. And it is said: 'Happy is the man who does this, and the human being who holds fast to it, who guards Shabbat against desecration and keeps his hand from doing any evil.' From this we learn that keeping Shabbat is as though keeping the whole Torah. Blessed be the Lord forever! Amen and amen.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Prayer for the Three Pilgrimage Festivals.

On each of the three pilgrimage festivals, before the evening prayer and at Shacharit after 'He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High,' and on the intermediate days after the Kaddish following Mussaf, recite the psalm appropriate to the festival.
Order of the Redemption of the Firstborn Son.
The priest takes the child and asks the father:

The priest asks: 'Is this son of yours a firstborn?' The father answers: 'Yes.' The priest asks him: 'Which would you rather have: your firstborn son, or the five sela'im with which you are obligated to redeem him?' The father answers: 'My firstborn son.' The priest then asks the child's mother: 'Is this son your firstborn? Perhaps you bore another son before him, or perhaps you suffered a miscarriage?' She answers: 'This is my firstborn son; I neither gave birth nor miscarried before him.' Then the priest says: 'This boy is a firstborn, and the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded that he be redeemed, as it is said: You shall redeem those to be redeemed from a month old, according to your valuation, for five shekels of silver by the sanctuary shekel, which is twenty gerahs. When you were in your mother's womb you were under the authority of your Father in heaven and of your father and mother. Now you are under my authority, for I am a priest, and your father and mother seek to redeem you, because you are a consecrated firstborn, as it is written: The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Sanctify to Me every firstborn, whatever opens the womb among the children of Israel, of man and of beast: it is Mine.'
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: The father then holds the coins or their monetary equivalent in his hand and says:

I wish to redeem him, as it is written in the Torah: 'You shall surely redeem the firstborn of humankind. At one month old you shall redeem him according to your valuation: five shekels of silver by the sacred shekel, each shekel twenty gerahs.'
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Before the blessing, he says this 'For the sake of the unification' declaration, then blesses:

For the sake of the unity of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Presence, in awe and love and in love and awe, to unite the letters Yod–Heh with Vav–Heh in perfect unity, in the name of all Israel: I now come to fulfill the positive commandment to redeem a firstborn son, as it is written: 'And all the firstborn of man among your sons shall you redeem,' and also: 'Those who are to be redeemed, from a month old, you shall redeem according to your valuation, for five shekels of silver by the sanctuary shekel, which is twenty gerahs.' May this be accounted before You as though I had fulfilled it with all its requirements, precise details, intentions and the commandments bound up with it, repairing its root in the supernal realm, to bring delight to my Maker and fulfill my Creator's will. May the favor of the Lord our God be upon us; establish the work of our hands for us; establish the work of our hands.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of a firstborn son.
Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this season.
Give it to the priest and say:
This is the redemption of my firstborn son.
The priest receives the money and says:
I have received from you these five sela coins for the redemption of this son of yours; he is thereby redeemed according to the law of Moses and Israel.

May it be Your will, LORD our God and God of our ancestors, that just as this son has merited redemption, so may he merit Torah, commandments, marriage and good deeds in the lifetimes of his father and mother. Amen; so may it be Your will.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Blessing upon building a safety parapet.

A person who builds a house has a positive commandment to install a guardrail around the roof. Even when the roof is rarely used, if the building below is a permanent dwelling it requires a guardrail. Leaving the roof unguarded neglects a positive commandment and violates a prohibition. If the building below is only a storage shed or the like, intended for temporary use, the roof does not require a guardrail (Ben Ish Chai, year 2, Pinchas 1).
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to make a parapet.
Blessing for immersing utensils.
Someone who purchases metal or glass eating utensils from a non-Jew must immerse them in a mikveh or spring containing forty seah of water.
Before immersing the vessels, while still outside the mikveh, recite the blessing:

Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the immersion of a utensil. For more than one utensil, say “utensils” in the plural.
Order of the second Shabbat meal.

When entering his home, a person stands at the place where he will sit for the morning Shabbat meal and circles the table once. He takes two bundles of myrtle (one for 'Remember' and one for 'Observe'), blesses them and smells them, saying aloud: 'Remember and observe were spoken in one utterance.' He also says quietly: 'A pleasing aroma, a fire offering to the LORD.' Still holding the myrtle, he circles the table a second time in silence. If no myrtle is available, other fragrant plants may be used.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Recite the following mishnayot from tractate Kelim, chapter 1, mishnah 6.

6. There are ten degrees of holiness. The Land of Israel is holier than all other lands. In what does its holiness consist? The omer offering, first fruits, and two loaves may be brought only from its produce; they may not be brought from produce grown in other lands. 7. Cities surrounded by walls are holier than the rest of the land: people afflicted with tzaraat are sent away from them. A dead body may be carried within the city until those carrying it decide to take it out, but once removed it may not be brought back. 8. The area within Jerusalem's walls is holier still: offerings of lesser sanctity and second tithe may be eaten there. The Temple Mount is holier: men and women with discharges, menstruating women and women after childbirth may not enter it. The hel, the inner enclosure, is holier: gentiles and those made impure by contact with the dead may not enter. The Women's Court is holier: those who have immersed but are waiting for sunset may not enter; however, violating this rule does not require a sin offering. The Court of Israel is holier: one who has not yet brought the required purification sacrifice may not enter, and violating this rule incurs a sin offering. The Court of the Priests is holier still: ordinary Israelites may enter only when necessary, to lay hands upon a sacrifice, to slaughter it, or to wave an offering. 9. The space between the porch and the altar is holier: priests with bodily blemishes or untrimmed, disheveled hair may not enter. The Temple building itself is holier: no one may enter without first washing hands and feet. The Holy of Holies is holiest of all: only the High Priest may enter it on Yom Kippur during the service. Rabbi Yose says: in five respects the area between the porch and altar has the same sanctity as the Temple building: those with bodily defects, with unkempt hair, who have drunk wine, or who have not washed hands and feet may not enter; and during the offering of incense everyone withdraws from that space.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Then recite the first mishnah of chapter 2, so as not to stop at a chapter boundary.

Chapter Two. Wooden utensils, leather utensils, bone utensils, and glass utensils: their flat forms are ritually pure, while their receptacles are susceptible to impurity. If they are broken, they become pure. If one subsequently makes utensils from them again, they become susceptible to impurity from that time onward. Earthenware and natron-clay utensils have the same rules of impurity: they become impure, and transmit impurity, through their interior airspace; they may become impure from contact with their outer surfaces, but not from contact with their backs; and breaking them renders them pure.
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Recite 'Let Israel now say'—this Zohar passage discusses the greatness of the Shabbat meals.

On Shabbat, at the second meal, it is written: 'Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord.' Specifically 'in the Lord,' for the Holy Ancient One is revealed at that time and all the worlds dwell in joy and perfection. We prepare the joy of the Ancient One, and this is truly His meal. Of Shabbat's third meal it says: 'I shall make you enjoy the heritage of Jacob your father.' This is the meal of the Lesser Countenance in its fullness, from whose fullness the six days of the week receive blessing. A person should rejoice in His meal and fulfill all three meals, for they are the meals of perfect faith belonging to the holy offspring of Israel. This lofty faith belongs to them and not to the peoples who worship idols, hence the verse: 'Between Me and the children of Israel.' Come and see: through these meals Israel are known as the King's children, dwellers in the King's palace, children of faith. Whoever omits even one of these meals shows a lack of perfection above, as though declaring that he is not a child of the Supreme King, does not belong to His palace or to the holy seed of Israel. A harsh decree is pronounced upon him, associated with three punishments, including the judgment of Gehinnom. Come and see: on other festivals a person must rejoice and bring joy to the poor. If he rejoices only himself and gives nothing to the poor, his punishment is severe: he feasts alone and does not share his joy. Of him it is said, 'I shall scatter dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals.' But one who rejoices on Shabbat, even without giving to others, is not punished in the same way as on other festivals, for the verse speaks of 'your festivals,' not 'your Shabbats.' And it is written: 'Your new moons and your festivals My soul hates'; Shabbat is not mentioned. Hence: 'Between Me and the children of Israel.' Because Shabbat contains the fullness of faith, a person receives another soul, a supernal soul perfected in the likeness of the world to come. For this reason the day is called Shabbat. What is Shabbat? It is the name of the Holy One, blessed be He, perfect in every respect. Rabbi Yose said, 'Indeed, it is so.' Woe to a person who does not complete the joy of the Holy King! In what does His joy consist? In the three meals of faith, which include the meals of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. All three rejoice in complete faith from every side. It has been taught: on this day the patriarchs are adorned with crowns and all the children receive nourishment, unlike on other festivals. On this day the wicked of Gehinnom rest; all judgments are subdued and do not awaken in the world; Torah is crowned with perfect crowns; joy and delight are given throughout two hundred and fifty worlds. Blessed be the Lord forever! Amen and amen.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Prepare the meal of perfect faith, the joy of the Holy King. Prepare the meal of the King: this is the meal of the Holy Ancient One (and the Field of Holy Apples and Zeir Anpin come to dine with Him).
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: The Ari established that this psalm be recited during the meal, though the general custom is to recite it before Kiddush. If Kiddush must be made quickly, recite this hymn during the meal (Ben Ish Hai, Bereshit 29).
The hymn 'Asader LiSeudata' by our teacher the Ari. Its acrostic spells: Ani Yitzchak Luria ('I am Isaac Luria').
I shall prepare for the meal on Shabbat morning, and now invite to it the Holy Ancient One.
May His light rest here in the great Kiddush, and may the soul rejoice in fine wine.
May He send us His beauty, that we may behold His glory, and reveal to us His secret that is spoken in a whisper.
May He reveal to us the meanings of the twelve loaves, which are a sign in His name, doubled and delicate.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: The bond above, in which all life resides: may strength grow and rise up to the head.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Rejoice, reapers of the field, in speech and voice; speak the word that is concealed in its garment.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Before the Master of the worlds, reveal sayings in hidden words, and proclaim a new interpretation.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: To crown the table with a precious secret, deep and concealed, not with words spoken aloud.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May these words be in the heavens; and who resides there? Behold, that sun.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: May abundant greatness increase above its rank, and may He take His consort, who was separated.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Before washing the fingertips after the meal, recite the following (Sha'ar HaKavanot, 74d):
I wash my hands before a single vessel, rejecting the other side, which has no substance.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: I make the invitation in three, with the cup of blessing, to the Cause of all causes, the Holy Ancient One.
paragraphs.note: New source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading outstanding.

paragraphs.text: Then recite the entire request 'Yehei Rava,' since it is beneficial to say this prayer before each of the three Shabbat meals (Sha'ar HaKavanot 71b).

May it be the will of the Holy Ancient One, the Holiest of all the holy, the most Concealed of the concealed and most Unknowable of all, that the supernal dew flow forth from Him, fill the head of the Lesser Countenance, and illuminate the field of holy apple trees with the radiance of His face, bestowing favor and joy upon all. From the Holy Ancient One, the Holiest of the holy, the most Concealed and Hidden of all, may favor and mercy, love and kindness, supernal light, good will and joy descend upon me, all my household, everyone connected with me, and all His people Israel. May He rescue us from all cruel oppression that could come into the world. May good food and honorable livelihood, without sorrow or want, be appointed and granted to us from the source of fortune on which all sustenance depends. May He save us from the evil eye, the sword of the angel of death, and the judgment of Gehinnom. May He send to us and to all our souls grace and goodness, long life, abundant provision and mercy from Himself. Amen, may it be His will. Amen and amen.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: It is appropriate to recite this Zohar passage from Parashat Vayakhel, folio 207b, before the daytime Kiddush.

The sanctification of the day, as has been established, is simply 'Creator of the fruit of the vine,' and nothing more. For the day stands sanctified in itself; this is not so with the night, which we must sanctify with these words, as we have explained. That night is sanctified only through the holy people below, when the supernal spirit rests upon them. We must sanctify it with the desire of the heart and direct our intention toward it. But the day sanctifies itself, and Israel are sanctified by their prayers and supplications and through the holiness of this day. Fortunate is Israel, the holy people, who inherited this day as an everlasting heritage. Blessed be the Lord forever, amen and amen.
paragraphs.note: Source-aligned English working translation; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Torah reading for public fast days.

And Moses besought the LORD his God, and said: ‘LORD, why doth Thy wrath wax hot against Thy people, that Thou hast brought forth out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand? Wherefore should the Egyptians speak, saying: For evil did He bring them forth, to slay them in the mountains, and to consume them from the face of the earth? Turn from Thy fierce wrath, and repent of this evil against Thy people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, Thy servants, to whom Thou didst swear by Thine own self, and saidst unto them: I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have spoken of will I give unto your seed, and they shall inherit it for ever.’ And the LORD repented of the evil which He said He would do unto His people. And the LORD said unto Moses: ‘Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first; and I will write upon the tables the words that were on the first tables, which thou didst break. And be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning unto mount Sinai, and present thyself there to Me on the top of the mount. And no man shall come up with thee, neither let any man be seen throughout all the mount; neither let the flocks nor herds feed before that mount.’ And he hewed two tables of stone like unto the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up unto mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand two tables of stone. And the LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD. And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed: ‘The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth; keeping mercy unto the thousandth generation, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin; and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children’s children, unto the third and unto the fourth generation.’ And Moses made haste, and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshipped. And he said: ‘If now I have found grace in Thy sight, O Lord, let the Lord, I pray Thee, go in the midst of us; for it is a stiffnecked people; and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for Thine inheritance.’ And He said: ‘Behold, I make a covenant; before all thy people I will do marvels, such as have not been wrought in all the earth, nor in any nation; and all the people among which thou art shall see the work of the LORD that I am about to do with thee, that it is tremendous.
paragraphs.note: Public-domain JPS 1917 English aligned with the original Hebrew; any liturgical instructions are supplied by the project.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Shabbat selections for the second meal.

Chapter 9. 1. Rabbi Akiva said: how do we know that an idol imparts ritual impurity when carried, like a woman during niddah? It says, 'Cast them away as an unclean thing; say to it, Away!' Just as a woman in niddah renders the person carrying her impure, so an object of idolatry renders its bearer impure. 2. How do we know that a ship does not contract ritual impurity? It says, 'The path of a ship in the midst of the sea.' How do we know that five kinds of seeds may be planted in a garden bed six handbreadths by six, four along its sides and one in the middle? It says, 'As the earth brings forth its shoots and a garden makes its seeds grow.' Scripture says not 'seed' in the singular, but 'seeds' in the plural. 3. How do we know that a woman who discharges semen on the third day becomes ritually impure? It says, 'Be ready for the third day.' How do we know that the place of circumcision may be washed on the third day, even when it falls on Shabbat? It says, 'On the third day, when they were in pain.' Why is a crimson thread tied to the head of the scapegoat? It says, 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.' 4. How do we know that anointing the body with oil on Yom Kippur is like drinking? Although this is not a direct proof, Scripture hints at it: 'It entered into his body like water, and like oil into his bones.' 5. The quantity of wood that makes one liable when carried is enough to cook an egg that cooks quickly; of spices, enough to season such an egg; different spices combine to reach the measure. Of nutshells, pomegranate peel, indigo, and madder, enough to dye a small piece of cloth used for headwear. Of urine, natron, soap, kimolia, or alkaline cleansing substance, enough to wash such a cloth. Rabbi Yehudah says: enough to remove a stain. 6. Of pepper, any amount; of pitch, any amount; of incense and metals, any amount. Likewise any amount of stones from the altar, its dust, or the dust of decayed sacred scrolls and their wrappings, since these are all kept for burial in a genizah. Rabbi Yehudah adds even the smallest part of an idolatrous object, as it says, 'Let nothing of the devoted thing cling to your hand.' 7. One who carries a merchant's box containing many objects brings only one sin offering. For garden seeds the minimum quantity is less than the volume of a dried fig; Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira says five seeds; for cucumber seeds, two; pumpkin seeds, two; Egyptian beans, two. For a live clean locust, any amount, but for a dead one, the volume of a dried fig. For a vineyard bird, living or dead, any amount because it is kept as medicine. Rabbi Yehudah says the same of a live unclean locust, for it is kept as a child's plaything.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 10. 1. One who has set something aside for sowing, as a sample or for medicine and then carries it out on Shabbat is liable regardless of its quantity. Everyone else is liable only for the established minimum quantity. If the first person brings the item back inside, liability henceforth applies only at the ordinary minimum measure. 2. One who carries food out and puts it on a threshold is exempt, whether he carries it farther himself or another person does so: the entire prohibited act was not performed as a single action. If he puts a full basket of fruit on an outer threshold, even if most of the basket projects outside, he is not liable until the whole basket is taken out. 3. One who carries something in the right or left hand, in the fold of a garment or on a shoulder is liable, for this is how the descendants of Kohath carried their burdens. One who carries it on the back of the hand, with the foot, mouth, elbow, ear, in the hair, in an inverted bag, between a bag and a shirt, in a shirt hem, shoe or sandal is exempt from bringing an offering, because people do not normally carry things this way. 4. If a person intended to carry something in front of him but it ended up behind his back, he is exempt; if he intended to carry it behind him but it ended up in front, he is liable. They said that a woman wearing an apron is liable whether it has moved to the front or to the back, since it normally turns around the body. Rabbi Yehudah includes those who receive written messages. 5. One who carries bread into the public domain is liable. If two people carry it together, both are exempt. If neither could carry it alone but they carried it together, both are liable; Rabbi Shimon exempts them. One who carries food less than the prescribed measure in a vessel is also exempt for the vessel, since it is subordinate to the food. One who carries a living person on a stretcher is exempt for both the person and the stretcher as its accessory. One who carries a corpse on a stretcher is liable, as also for carrying an olive's bulk of flesh from a corpse or animal carcass or a lentil's bulk of a dead creeping creature; Rabbi Shimon exempts him. 6. One who cuts his nails with other nails or his teeth, plucks hair, mustache or beard, braids hair, applies eye cosmetics or arranges a hairstyle is liable for violating Torah law according to Rabbi Eliezer; the sages prohibit these acts as shevut, a rabbinic restriction. One who uproots a plant from a perforated pot is liable; from an unperforated pot he is exempt. Rabbi Shimon exempts him in both cases.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 11. 1. One who throws an object from a private domain into a public one, or from a public domain into a private one, is liable. If he throws from one private domain to another over a public domain, Rabbi Akiva holds him liable, but the sages exempt him. 2. How so? Two balconies face one another on opposite sides of a public area. One who extends or throws an object from one to the other is exempt. If both balconies are on the same level, one who hands over an object is liable, but one who throws it is exempt. This was the practice of the Levites: two wagons stood one behind the other on the public road, and beams were passed from wagon to wagon, not thrown. If the rim of a well or a rock stands ten handbreadths high and is four handbreadths wide, one who takes an object from it or puts something on it is liable; if its dimensions are less, one is exempt. 3. One who throws an object four cubits against a wall above ten handbreadths from the ground is considered to have thrown it into the air; below ten, to have thrown it onto the ground. One who throws an object four cubits along the ground is liable. If one threw it less than four cubits but it rolled farther, one is exempt; if one threw it farther than four cubits and it rolled back nearer, one is liable. 4. One who throws an object four cubits in the sea is exempt. If a shallow puddle lies on a public road and people walk through it, someone throwing an object four cubits across it is liable. Shallow water means less than ten handbreadths deep. If the road passes through such water, throwing across four cubits incurs liability. 5. One who throws from sea to land, land to sea, sea to ship, ship to sea, or ship to ship is exempt. Between two ships that are tied together one may transfer objects. If they are not tied, even though they touch, transfer is prohibited. 6. If a person throws an object and remembers Shabbat after it has left his hand, or another person catches it, a dog seizes it, or it burns, he is exempt. If someone throws something intending to injure a person or animal but recalls the prohibition before injury occurs, he is exempt. The general principle is that an offering for an unintentional violation is due only where both the beginning and the completion of the act were unintentional. If its beginning was unintentional and its completion deliberate, or conversely, there is no obligation to bring such an offering.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 12. 1. For how much building is one liable? For any amount, even the smallest. A person who dresses a stone, strikes with a hammer or adze, or drills a hole is liable for any completed act. The general rule is that one who performs a kind of work on Shabbat whose result is lasting is liable. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that even a craftsman who strikes his hammer on the anvil during work is liable, because in this way he prepares his tool. 2. One is liable for plowing even the smallest area, weeding, cutting branches or pruning young shoots in any quantity. One who gathers firewood to improve the land is liable for any amount; if gathering it for fuel, only for enough to cook an egg that cooks quickly. For gathering grass to improve the land, any amount; for feeding an animal, enough to fill the mouth of a kid goat. 3. One who writes two letters with either the right or left hand, whether the letters are identical or different, with two kinds of ink, or in any language, is liable. Rabbi Yose says that the liability for writing two letters primarily concerns making marks, for marks were made on the boards of the Tabernacle so that one would know which board was to be joined to which. Rabbi says: a short word may be found within a long one, such as 'Shem' in 'Shimon' or 'Shmuel,' 'Noah' in 'Nahor,' 'Dan' in 'Daniel,' or 'Gad' in 'Gadiel.' 4. Whoever writes two letters during one period of unawareness of the prohibition is liable. This concerns writing with ink, dye, red paint, gum, vitriol or any substance that leaves a permanent mark; also on two adjoining walls of a corner or two pages of a notebook if the characters may be read together. One who writes on his own skin is liable. Regarding one who scratches letters into skin, Rabbi Eliezer requires a sin offering and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. 5. Whoever writes with liquid, fruit juice, road dust, scribes' powder or any other impermanent substance is exempt. So is one who writes using the back of the hand, the foot, mouth or elbow; adds one letter to an existing word; writes over existing writing; intended to write one letter het but wrote two zayins; wrote one letter on the ground and another on a beam; or wrote on two walls or pages which cannot be read together. If one wrote a single letter as an abbreviation, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira holds him liable, but the sages exempt him. 6. If one wrote two letters during two separate periods of ignorance of the prohibition, one in the morning and one in the evening, Rabban Gamliel holds him liable and the sages exempt him.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 13. 1. Rabbi Eliezer says: one who first weaves three threads, or adds one thread to a finished fabric, is liable. The sages say that both at the beginning and at the end the minimum quantity is two threads. 2. One who makes two loops for heddles on a loom, frame, sieve, strainer or basket is liable; likewise one who makes two stitches or tears cloth in order to sew it with two stitches. 3. One who tears garments in anger or in mourning for the dead, like anyone whose act is merely destructive, is exempt from a sin offering. One who destroys for the sake of repairing is liable for the same minimum quantity as one who carries out the repair. 4. The minimum measure for bleaching, combing fibers, dyeing and spinning is twice the width of the outstretched fingers; for weaving two threads, the width of outstretched fingers. 5. Rabbi Yehudah says: whoever traps a bird in a tower or a deer in a house is liable. The sages say: a bird in a tower, or a deer in a house, a courtyard or an enclosure. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: not all enclosures are alike. This is the rule: if the animal still needs to be caught, the person is exempt; if it no longer needs catching, he is liable. 6. If a deer entered a house and one person shut the door behind it, that person is liable. If two people shut the door together, both are exempt; but if neither could shut it alone and they did so together, both are liable. Rabbi Shimon exempts them. 7. If one person sat in a doorway but did not block it completely, and another sat down and closed the opening, the second is liable. If the first person completely blocked the opening at once, and the second sat beside him, then even if the first later got up and left, only the first is liable. This is like someone who closed a house to guard it and thereby also guarded the deer that was inside.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 14. 1. Of the eight kinds of creeping animals mentioned in the Torah, one who captures or wounds them on Shabbat is liable. A person who wounds other creeping creatures is exempt; one who captures them for a particular use is liable, but if there is no such use is exempt. One who captures domesticated wild animals or birds is exempt, but one who wounds them is liable. 2. Strong brine may not be prepared on Shabbat, although salted water may be made for dipping bread and adding to food. Rabbi Yose objects: is brine not brine whether prepared in large or small quantities? Permitted salted water is prepared by placing oil first into either the water or the salt. 3. Medicinal hyssop must not be eaten on Shabbat because healthy people do not ordinarily eat it, but one may eat yo'ezer and drink the shepherd's-flute preparation. Generally one may eat ordinary foods and drink ordinary beverages even for healing, except palm water and a preparation for infertility used against jaundice. Palm water may be drunk to quench thirst, and one may apply the infertility oil when not using it medicinally. 4. Someone with a toothache must not rinse the mouth with vinegar as a treatment, but may dip food in vinegar as usual; if it relieves the pain, so be it. One with back pain must not rub the back with wine or vinegar, but may apply oil other than rose oil. Princes may apply rose oil to their wounds since they use it on weekdays as well. Rabbi Shimon says: All Israelites are like the children of kings.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 14, source-aligned full working English translation.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 15. 1. For which knots is one liable on Shabbat? The camel driver's knot and the sailor's knot. Just as one is liable for tying them, so one is liable for untying them. Rabbi Meir says that if a knot can be untied with one hand, one is not liable for it. 2. There are knots for which one is not liable as for the camel driver's or sailor's knot. A woman may tie the slit of her shirt, the ribbons of her headdress, her belt, the straps of a shoe or sandal, the mouths of wine and oil skins, and a container of meat. Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob says that an animal may be tied up to prevent its escape. A bucket may be fastened with a belt but not a rope; Rabbi Judah permits a rope. Rabbi Judah stated this rule: one is not liable for any knot that is not intended to be permanent. 3. Garments may be folded even four or five times, and beds may be made from the beginning of Shabbat for the needs of Shabbat, but not on Shabbat in preparation for the evening after it. Rabbi Ishmael says that garments may be folded and beds made on Yom Kippur for Shabbat, and that the fat portions of Sabbath offerings may be burned on Yom Kippur, but not those of Yom Kippur on Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva says that neither the fat of Sabbath offerings is burned on Yom Kippur, nor the fat of Yom Kippur on Shabbat.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 15, complete working translation checked against the bundled Hebrew and Russian.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 16. 1. All sacred writings may be saved from a fire on Shabbat, whether or not they are publicly read. Even those written in another language must be stored properly in a genizah. Why may certain writings not be read at that time? So as not to interrupt study in the study house. One may save a scroll case together with its scroll and a tefillin case together with its tefillin, even if money is inside. Where may they be carried for safety? Into a blind alley that does not run through from end to end. Ben Beteira also permits a thoroughfare. 2. Food for three meals may be rescued: for people, food fit for people; for animals, food fit for them. If a fire breaks out on Shabbat night, one may rescue enough food for three meals; in the morning, for two; at Minchah, for one. Rabbi Yose says: food for three meals may always be rescued. 3. One may rescue a basket of bread even if it suffices for a hundred meals, a cake of dried figs and a barrel of wine. One may say to others, 'Come and save food for yourselves.' If they are sensible, they will settle accounts with the owner after Shabbat. Where may the rescued goods be taken? Into a courtyard encompassed by an eruv. Ben Beteira also permits taking them into a courtyard without an eruv. 4. One may also carry necessary household utensils there, putting on as many garments and wrapping oneself in as many coverings as possible. Rabbi Yose sets a limit of eighteen articles of clothing. One may return, dress again, carry more out, and tell others, 'Come and help me save things.' 5. Rabbi Shimon ben Nanas says that a goatskin may be spread over a chest, coffer or wardrobe threatened by flames, because the skin merely chars. One may form a barrier of any vessels, full or empty, to keep fire from spreading. Rabbi Yose forbids putting out new earthenware vessels full of water, since the heat will crack them and the water will extinguish the fire. 6. If a non-Jew comes to put out a fire, one neither tells him 'Put it out' nor 'Do not put it out,' since he is not obligated to observe our Shabbat rest. If a child comes to extinguish it, however, one does not allow him, for adults are responsible for his Shabbat rest. 7. One may invert a bowl over a lamp so that it will not set a beam alight, over a child's excrement, or over a scorpion so it will not sting. Rabbi Yehudah said: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai adjudicated such a case in Arav and feared that the person was liable to bring a sin offering. 8. If a non-Jew lights a lamp for himself, a Jew may use its light; if he lights it for a Jew, it may not be used. If a non-Jew draws water for his own animal, a Jew may water his animal afterward; if he drew it for a Jew, it may not be used. If a non-Jew makes a gangway to disembark from a ship, a Jew may use it afterward; if it was made for a Jew, he may not. It is related that Rabban Gamliel and the elders were sailing on a ship, and a non-Jew set up a gangway to go ashore; Rabban Gamliel and the elders used it.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Shabbat study for the third Shabbat meal.

Prepare the meal of perfect faith, the joy of the Holy King. Prepare the King’s meal: this is the meal of the holy King, the Radiant Countenance (with the Holy Ancient One and the field of holy apples coming to dine with Him).

Chapter 18. 1. For the sake of guests or to prevent interruption of study in the study house, even four or five baskets of straw or grain may be cleared away, but not an entire storehouse. One may move ritually pure terumah, demai (produce of doubtful tithing), first tithe from which the contribution has been separated, redeemed second tithe and consecrated produce, and dry lupines that are food for the poor. One must not move tevel (untithed produce), first tithe whose contribution has not been separated, unredeemed second tithe or consecrated produce, or arum and mustard plants. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits moving arum, because it serves as food for ravens. 2. Bundles of straw, wood and shoots may be moved if they have been set aside as animal feed, but not otherwise. An overturned basket may be set before chicks so they can climb in and out. A hen that strays may be pushed back into its coop. Calves and young horses may be supported while walking, even in the public domain. A woman may help her child walk. Rabbi Judah explains that this is permitted when the child lifts one foot and sets the other down; if the child drags both feet it is forbidden. 3. On a festival one may not deliver an animal's young, but may assist the animal during labor. On Shabbat one may assist a woman giving birth, bring a midwife from elsewhere and override Shabbat prohibitions to preserve her life; the umbilical cord may be tied. Rabbi Yose even permits cutting it. Everything necessary for circumcision may be performed on Shabbat.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 18, source-aligned full working English translation.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 19. 1. Rabbi Eliezer says: if the implement for circumcision was not brought before Shabbat began, it may be brought openly on Shabbat, or in a time of danger, covered and in the presence of witnesses. Rabbi Eliezer also permits cutting down trees to produce charcoal for forging an iron implement. Rabbi Akiva laid down this rule: any work that could have been done on the eve of Shabbat must not be done on Shabbat; what could not be done in advance overrides Shabbat restrictions. 2. All necessities of circumcision may be performed on Shabbat: making the incision, uncovering the glans, drawing away blood, and applying a dressing and cumin. If the cumin was not ground beforehand, one may chew it with the teeth and apply it. If wine and oil were not mixed in advance, they may be applied separately. A special wrapping may not be made for the first time on Shabbat, but one may bind the area with a piece of cloth. If the cloth was not prepared beforehand, it may be wrapped around a finger and brought even from another courtyard. 3. An infant may be washed both before and after circumcision; water may be sprinkled with the hand but not from a vessel. Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah permits washing an infant on the third day after circumcision even if it is Shabbat, since it says, 'On the third day, when they were in pain.' If there is doubt as to whether circumcision is required, or the infant has sexual characteristics of both sexes, Shabbat may not be violated for that purpose; Rabbi Yehudah permits it in the latter case. 4. If a man has two infants, one due to be circumcised after Shabbat and one on Shabbat, and he mistakenly circumcises on Shabbat the one whose time is after Shabbat, he is liable. If one infant should have been circumcised before Shabbat and the other on Shabbat, but he mistakenly circumcises the former on Shabbat, Rabbi Eliezer requires a sin offering, whereas Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. 5. A baby may be circumcised on the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh or twelfth day, neither earlier nor later in these circumstances. Ordinarily it is on the eighth day; one born at twilight is circumcised on the ninth; one born at twilight before Shabbat, on the tenth. If a festival follows Shabbat, on the eleventh; if two festival days of Rosh Hashanah intervene, on the twelfth. An ill child is not circumcised until he recovers. 6. What remnants of foreskin invalidate a circumcision? Those which cover most of the crown. Until the defect is corrected the person may not eat terumah. If extra flesh makes it appear that he is uncircumcised, it is removed for the sake of proper appearance. One who made the incision but did not uncover the crown is regarded as not having performed circumcision at all.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 20. 1. Rabbi Eliezer says that a wine strainer may be suspended on a festival, and wine may be poured through one already suspended on Shabbat. The Sages say that the strainer may not be suspended on a festival and wine may not be poured through it on Shabbat, though pouring through one already suspended is permitted on a festival. 2. Water may be poured over wine sediment to clarify it; wine may be filtered through cloth or an Egyptian basket; an egg may be placed in a mustard strainer; and spiced honey-wine called anomelin may be prepared on Shabbat. Rabbi Judah says that on Shabbat only a cupful may be prepared, on a festival a jugful, and on the intermediate festival days a barrelful. Rabbi Zadok says the amount depends upon the number of guests. 3. Asafoetida must not be steeped in lukewarm water, but it may be placed in vinegar. Fodder beans may not be soaked or rubbed, but may be placed in a sieve or basket. Straw must not be sifted nor raised high to scatter the chaff, but it may be taken in a sieve and transferred to a manger. 4. According to Rabbi Dosa, one may sweep the space before fattened livestock and move aside refuse in front of other animals. The Sages prohibit this. Food may be transferred from one animal to another on Shabbat. 5. Straw on a bed must not be shaken out by hand but may be moved with the body. If the straw is fit for animal feed, or if a pillow or sheet lies over it, it may be adjusted by hand. A household clothes press may be opened but must not be tightened; a professional launderer's press must not be touched. Rabbi Judah says that if it was loosened before Shabbat it may be fully opened and the garment taken out.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 20, source-aligned full working English translation.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 21. 1. A person may carry a child who is holding a stone, or a basket containing a stone. Ritually impure terumah may be moved together with pure terumah or with ordinary food. Rabbi Judah says that one may even separate terumah from a mixture when there are one hundred parts of ordinary produce to one part of terumah. 2. If a stone lies on the mouth of a barrel, tilt the barrel to the side and let the stone fall. If the barrel stands among others, pick it up, carry it away, then tilt it so the stone falls. If coins lie on a pillow, shake the pillow so the coins fall off. If bird droppings are on a cushion, wipe them off with a rag; if the cushion is made of leather, pour water over it until the dirt is removed. 3. The School of Shammai says that one may remove bones and husks from the table. The School of Hillel says that one should lift the entire tabletop and shake it off. Crumbs smaller than an olive, and pea and lentil pods, may be removed because they can serve as feed for animals. If a sponge has a leather handle it may be used for wiping; if it has no handle it may not. The Sages say that in either case it may be moved on Shabbat, and it does not contract ritual impurity.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 21, complete working translation checked against the bundled Hebrew and Russian.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 22. 1. If a barrel breaks, one may rescue enough of its contents for three meals, and say to others, 'Come and save some for yourselves,' but may not use a sponge to absorb its liquid. Fruit may not be squeezed for juice; juice that runs out by itself may not be used. Rabbi Judah says that if the fruit was intended for eating, the liquid that emerges by itself is permitted, but if it was intended for drinking, that liquid is forbidden. Honey that seeps by itself from combs crushed before Shabbat is forbidden, whereas Rabbi Eliezer permits it. 2. Something cooked in hot water before Shabbat may be soaked in hot water on Shabbat. Something not previously cooked may only be rinsed in hot water, except for aged salted fish, small salted fish and Spanish tuna, which are considered cooked even by rinsing. 3. A barrel may be broken to obtain dried figs, provided one does not intend to make a new vessel. Rabbi Judah prohibits piercing its lid; the Sages permit it. An opening must not be made in the barrel's side. An existing opening may not be sealed with wax, since that constitutes smoothing. Rabbi Judah reported that when such a case was discussed before Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai in Arav, he feared it might incur liability for a sin offering. 4. A prepared dish may be lowered into a well to preserve it, drinking water placed into cooler water to chill it, or cold water placed in the sun to warm. Someone whose clothes become wet on the road may continue walking in them without concern. Upon reaching the outer courtyard the clothes may be spread out in the sun, but not where others can see. 5. Someone who bathed in a cave or in the waters of Tiberias, and dried themselves with even ten towels, must not carry them in hand. But ten people may dry their faces, hands and feet with a single towel and carry it together. 6. On Shabbat one may anoint the body and gently massage the abdomen, but not perform therapeutic exercises or rub the body in a specialized medicinal manner. One must not go down into the Kurdima pool, induce vomiting, reset an infant's bones, or splint a fracture. Someone who dislocated a hand or foot must not rub it with cold water as treatment, but may wash it as usual; if the pain subsides, so be it.
paragraphs.note: Mishnah Shabbat chapter 22, source-aligned full working English translation.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 23. 1. A person may ask another for jugs of wine or oil, provided he does not use the expression 'lend me' in the sense of an ordinary commercial loan; likewise, a woman may ask her neighbor for bread. If the owner does not trust the borrower, a cloak may be left with him and accounts settled after Shabbat. Similarly in Jerusalem, on the eve of Passover falling on Shabbat, a person could leave his cloak as security, receive his Paschal offering, and pay after the festival. 2. A householder may enumerate his guests and dishes from memory, but may not read a written list. He may cast lots among his children and household members at the table, provided he does not deliberately set large portions against small ones, lest this resemble gambling. On a festival, lots may be drawn to distribute entitled portions of sacred offerings, but not separate portions of food. 3. One does not hire workers on Shabbat or ask another person to hire them. One may not wait at the edge of the Shabbat travel limit until dark in order immediately to hire workers or bring in fruit. One may, however, wait there to guard property and then bring in fruit with one's own hands. Abba Shaul formulated the rule: for anything I am permitted to discuss on Shabbat, I may wait at the boundary until Shabbat ends. 4. One may wait at the Shabbat boundary for matters connected with a wedding or the needs of the dead, such as a coffin or burial shrouds. If a non-Jew brings flutes on Shabbat, Jews may not use them at a mourning ceremony unless they were brought from nearby. If a coffin was made and a grave dug for a non-Jew, a Jew may be buried there; if made especially for a Jew, it may never be used. 5. All proper care of the body of the deceased is permitted: one may anoint and wash it, but not move the limbs. The pillow may be removed from beneath the body and the body placed on sand to preserve it until burial. The lower jaw may be tied up, not to raise it, but to keep it from falling farther. In the same way, a broken beam may be supported by a bench or the legs of a bed, not to raise it but to keep it from falling any further. One may not close the eyes of a deceased person on Shabbat, nor on a weekday at the moment the soul departs; whoever does this while the person is dying is as though he sheds blood.
paragraphs.note: New English working translation reviewed against the Hebrew and available Russian text; specialist proofreading pending.

paragraphs.text: Chapter 24. 1. If night falls upon someone traveling along a road, that person may give a purse to a non-Jew. If there is no non-Jew present, place it upon a donkey. On reaching an outer courtyard, remove from the donkey any articles that may be moved on Shabbat. As for those that may not be moved, undo the straps and let the sacks fall by themselves. 2. Bundles of stalks may be untied before livestock, and straw may be spread out, but compactly bound sheaves may not be loosened. Hay or carob pods may not be chopped for animals, whether large or small. Rabbi Judah allows chopping carobs for small livestock. 3. A camel must not have feed forced into its mouth or down its throat, although it may be fed normally. Calves may not be force-fed into the stomach, but food may be placed in their mouths. Grain may be offered to chickens. Water may be poured upon bran, but it may not be kneaded into a thick mixture. Water is not set out for bees or wild doves in a dovecote, but it may be set out for geese, chickens and domesticated doves. 4. Pumpkins may be cut for livestock and carrion for dogs. Rabbi Judah says that if an animal did not die before Shabbat began, its carcass must not be fed to dogs, for it was not prepared beforehand. 5. Vows may be annulled on Shabbat, and a sage consulted concerning vows relating to the needs of Shabbat. One may stop a window opening and measure cloth or a ritual bath. In the days of Rabbi Zadok's father and Abba Shaul ben Botnit, an opening for light was plugged with a jar and a measuring vessel was tied with a reed to determine whether an opening was a handbreadth wide. From this it was learned that closing openings, measuring, and tying necessary knots are permitted on Shabbat.
